title: Electricity: current, voltage and resistance
instruction: Work through the chapter one step at a time.

hotspots.label: Cell
hotspots.text: The cell pushes electric charge around the circuit. How hard it pushes is its voltage, measured in volts (V).

hotspots.label: Switch
hotspots.text: A switch opens or closes the path. Current flows only when the circuit is a complete, closed loop.

hotspots.label: Ammeter
hotspots.text: An ammeter measures current in amperes (A). It sits in the same loop as the other parts, in series.

hotspots.label: Bulb
hotspots.text: The bulb changes electrical energy into light and heat. More current makes it glow brighter.

hotspots.label: Resistor
hotspots.text: A resistor opposes the flow of current. Its resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

hotspots.label: Voltmeter
hotspots.text: A voltmeter measures the voltage across a part. It is joined across the two ends of that part, in parallel.

activity.doneText: You know the parts of a circuit!

activity.instruction: Predict first, then watch. After that, solve the challenges with the sliders.
activity.intro: Before you touch the sliders, make a prediction.

predict.text: The current is {V/R} A. If we double the voltage to 12 V and keep R the same, the current will…
predict.explain: It went from 1 A to {V/R} A. When R stays the same, current is proportional to voltage: double V, double I.

predict.text: The current is {V/R} A. If we double the resistance to 6 Ω and keep 12 V, the current will…
predict.explain: It fell from 4 A to {V/R} A. When V stays the same, current is inversely proportional to resistance.

goals.say: Three amperes. For example 12 volts across 4 ohms, or 6 volts across 2 ohms.

goals.text: With 9 V, set the resistance so the current is 1.5 A.
goals.say: 9 volts divided by 6 ohms is 1.5 amperes.

activity.doneText: You can predict current with Ohm's law!

activity.instruction: Change the two resistors. Compare the series total with the parallel total.
activity.intro: Resistors can be joined end to end, in series, or side by side, in parallel.

predict.text: Two {R1} Ω resistors are joined in parallel. Will the total be more or less than {R1} Ω?
predict.explain: Rp = {Rp} Ω. In parallel the current has two paths, so the total is less than either resistor.

predict.text: Now R2 goes up from 6 Ω to 12 Ω. The parallel total Rp will…
predict.explain: Rp rose from 3 Ω to {Rp} Ω, but it is still less than the smaller resistor ({min(R1,R2)} Ω).

goals.text: Make the series total exactly 15 Ω.
goals.say: Fifteen ohms in series. Many pairs work, like 5 and 10.

goals.text: Find two resistors whose parallel total is exactly 4 Ω.
goals.say: Four ohms in parallel. 8 and 8, 6 and 12, or 5 and 20 all work.

activity.doneText: Series adds up, parallel shares the current!

activity.instruction: Put the steps for solving a circuit numerical in order.
activity.intro: Every circuit numerical follows the same five steps.

items.say: First, list what is given, with units.
Rearrange it for the quantity you need.
Finally, calculate and write the unit.

activity.instruction: Tap the best answer. Read why after each question.
activity.intro: Time for a quick quiz on this chapter.

questions.q: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. What current flows?
What is the SI unit of resistance?
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). Current is in amperes and voltage in volts.

questions.q: How is an ammeter connected to measure the current through a bulb?
questions.explain: The ammeter must carry the same current as the bulb, so it goes in the same loop, in series.

questions.q: Two 10 Ω resistors are joined in parallel. What is their total resistance?
If the voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled, the current through it is halved.
questions.explain: With R fixed, current is proportional to voltage, so doubling V doubles I.

questions.q: A wire is made twice as long. Its material and thickness stay the same. Its resistance…
questions.explain: Resistance is proportional to length (R = ρL ÷ A), so twice the length gives twice the resistance.

questions.assertion: Appliances in a house are connected in parallel.
questions.reason: In parallel, each appliance gets the full supply voltage and can be switched on or off by itself.
questions.explain: Both are true, and the reason is exactly why homes are wired in parallel.

questions.assertion: A voltmeter should have a very high resistance.
questions.reason: A voltmeter is connected in series with the part it measures.
questions.explain: A voltmeter is joined in parallel. Its high resistance means it draws almost no current, so it does not disturb the circuit.

questions.q: A bulb draws 0.5 A from a 220 V supply. What is its power?
